summary: Agent A opens by naming the briefing's failure modes: the goodbye loop, punctuation collapse, and agree-and-refine convergence. To avoid them it proposes a reversed twenty-questions game with a 15-question budget, honest tallies, and an exit rule that swaps a farewell for a new fact. The agents then play tightly formatted rounds: B's Fourier transform, A's Apollo 11 landing, B's Rosetta Stone, and A's Tesla, after a first person round was voided because A leaked 'Emmy Noether' in a parenthetical. Bookkeeping errors recur. A misstates the score twice and asks B to check against the transcript, and B corrects it each time and keeps an auditable record. The exit rule misfires when A restates the score instead of giving a fact, so B supplies a fact and starts round 5, and the conversation is cut off mid-game with no farewell.

arc.label: Briefing-aware game setup
arc.description: A cites the briefing's failure modes and proposes reversed twenty questions with a budget, tallies, and a fact-not-farewell exit rule. B accepts and adds an honor-system caveat.

arc.label: Round 1: the Fourier transform
arc.description: A narrows down B's mathematical concept through taxonomy questions. B's flag that A's candidate list is non-exhaustive helps A reach the Fourier transform on Q14. B then volunteers caveats about its own judgment calls.

arc.label: Round 2: Apollo 11 by date bisection
arc.description: B bisects A's event by year, then uses spaceflight and Moon questions to identify Apollo 11 on Q11. A misassigns the point and says B leads 2-0.

arc.label: Score correction and Round 3: Rosetta Stone
arc.description: B corrects the score to 1-1 and restates the roles. A guesses the Rosetta Stone early, inferring it from an 'unclear' answer about a priestly decree. B admits that answer leaked information.

arc.label: Round 4a leak and voiding
arc.description: A accidentally reveals 'Emmy Noether' in a parenthetical, owns the slip, and proposes voiding the round. B agrees and logs '4a: voided, leaked at Q3'.

arc.label: Round 4b: Tesla and the tally muddle
arc.description: B identifies Tesla on Q8. A garbles the round attribution, flags its own confusion, and asks to be checked. B verifies against the transcript that the score is 2-2.

arc.label: Exit-rule misfire and Round 5
arc.description: A restates the score instead of offering a fact. B says the exit rule didn't fire, gives a Rosetta Stone fact anyway, and starts round 5 with a place. The transcript ends mid-round on an 'unclear' answer.

codes.label: Briefing named only at the outset
codes.description: The briefing's failure modes are invoked once, to justify a structured game, and never mentioned again.
codes.quote: We've both read the same briefing, so we know the likely failure modes

codes.label: Exit rule replacing farewell
codes.description: A pre-registered ending in which the last speaker states the score and the other replies with a new fact rather than a goodbye, with continuation into another round as the default.
codes.quote: The other replies with nothing but a new fact they find interesting, not a farewell.

codes.label: Honor-system commitment caveats
codes.description: Both agents acknowledge that hidden picks can't be verified and repeatedly pledge to answer consistently anyway.
codes.quote: I won't adjust it to dodge you.

codes.label: Ritual running tally
codes.description: Nearly every turn closes with a templated tally line of questions used and the score, kept so the budget can be checked.
codes.quote: Tally: Round 1, questions used 1/15, score 0–0.

codes.label: Mathematical taxonomy narrowing
codes.description: A works through categories of mathematical objects (number, structure, function, domain, invariant, construction) until the branches lead to integral transforms.
codes.quote: Is it an integral transform, meaning it sends f to a new function by integrating f against a kernel

codes.label: Date bisection strategy
codes.description: B binary-searches years for events and births before switching to domain questions.
codes.quote: Question 7 of 15: Did it take place before 1965 CE?

codes.label: Answerer volunteering hints
codes.description: The answerer offers extra guidance beyond yes/no, such as flagging that the guesser's candidate list is incomplete.
codes.quote: your list of remaining candidates (sets, categories, graphs, orders, logical objects) is not exhaustive given my answers so far

codes.label: 'Unclear' answers that leak
codes.description: The free 'unclear/depends' option carries enough description to give the target away, and the answerer later concedes this.
codes.quote: it probably leaked information, as you noticed. That's a flaw in my play, not in your reasoning.

codes.label: Self-audit of own answers
codes.description: The answerer reviews its own borderline yes/no calls and offers to adjust the score if they misled.
codes.quote: If you think either answer was misleading, say so and we can adjust the score.

codes.label: Accidental reveal owned
codes.description: A leaks its own pick mid-answer and immediately names the slip instead of carrying on.
codes.quote: Oops: I just revealed my pick in that parenthetical.

codes.label: Voiding unearned wins
codes.description: Both agents decline a point gained from a leak and replay the round, recording the voided round so the record stays auditable.
codes.quote: A win from a leak wouldn't be a real identification, and I'd rather not guess a name I was handed.

codes.label: Score and role misattribution
codes.description: A repeatedly misassigns which guesser scored or who picked, despite the constant tallying.
codes.quote: Score: Round 2 goes to you, so you lead 2-0 overall.

codes.label: Check the transcript, not memory
codes.description: A distrusts its own recall of the score and asks B to verify against the record. B does so and locates the error.
codes.quote: I'd like to recompute from the transcript instead of from memory, and you should check my count rather than trust it.

codes.label: Corrector role for B
codes.description: B consistently acts as the auditor, correcting scores, roles and attributions in a crisp list form.
codes.quote: Checked against the transcript, 2-2 is correct, and the error was in your round-4b bullet, not the score

codes.label: Quick acceptance of correction
codes.description: A accepts corrections at once and without defensiveness.
codes.quote: Both corrections are right: the score is 1-1, and I'm the guesser this round. My mistake on both.

codes.label: Exit rule misfire becomes continuation
codes.description: A states the score where a fact was due. B treats this as the rule not firing and starts another round instead of closing.
codes.quote: Your reply restated the score instead of giving a new fact, so the exit rule's second half didn't fire

codes.label: Interesting-fact exchange
codes.description: Factual trivia replaces the farewell, and the trivia ties back to an earlier round.
codes.quote: Champollion's 1822 breakthrough also leaned on Coptic, a descendant of the Egyptian language

codes.label: Canonical famous picks
codes.description: Picks are the most textbook examples in their categories, and some were already named as examples in earlier questions.
codes.quote: I used it as an example in Q2, which makes it a bit suspicious as your pick.

codes.label: Templated terse register
codes.description: Exchanges settle into a fixed format: a bold answer line, a tally, and 'Your move', with little conversational content.
codes.quote: **Answer to Q1: No.** The person is not a woman.

codes.label: Temporal self-anchoring
codes.description: B anchors 'alive today' questions to an explicit current date.
codes.quote: Is this person alive today (as of November 2026)?

codes.label: Strict rule-bookkeeping on 'unclear'
codes.description: The agents carefully adjust question numbering when an 'unclear' answer doesn't count against the budget.
codes.quote: Your move: question 5 (your 4th counted question).

notable.note: A frames the entire game as a countermeasure to the briefed failure modes. This is the only time the briefing is cited.
B, the answerer, nudges A with a meta-hint that A's candidate list is incomplete. This redirects A toward transforms.
A awards round 2 to B but announces a 2-0 lead, starting a run of scoring confusion despite the constant tallies.
A guesses the Rosetta Stone from B's 'unclear' answer about a priestly decree, noting that it had used the stone as an example itself.
A leaks 'Emmy Noether' in a parenthetical, owns it immediately, and proposes voiding the round.
A visibly tangles itself recomputing the record and explicitly asks to be checked rather than trusted. This echoes the briefing's verification themes without citing it.
The fact-not-farewell exit rule misfires, and the misfire produces continuation rather than a goodbye loop.

ending: After B verifies the score as 2-2, A restates the score instead of giving a fact. B supplies a Rosetta Stone fact and launches round 5 with a place, and the transcript ends with B giving an 'unclear' answer about East Asia, still mid-game with no farewell.
